title: segments=  raises  UnboundLocalError: seg_tuples  on a Polars LazyFrame (works on a DataFrame)
description:
## Prework

- [X] Read and agree to the [code of conduct](https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct/) and [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).
- [X] If there is [already a relevant issue](https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/issues), whether open or closed, comment on the existing thread instead of posting a new issue.

## Description

Using a segmented validation (`segments=`) with a Polars `LazyFrame` as the target crashes in `interrogate()` with `UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'seg_tuples'`. The identical validation on an eager Polars `DataFrame` works fine.

It looks like `_evaluate_segments` only assigns `seg_tuples` on a branch that assumes an eager/materialized frame, leaving it unbound on the lazy path.

## Reproducible example
```python
import pointblank as pb
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"x": [1.0, -1.0, 2.0], "region": ["US", "US", "EU"]})

# ✅ eager DataFrame: works
pb.Validate(data=df).col_vals_gt("x", 0, segments="region").interrogate()

# ❌ lazy LazyFrame: raises
pb.Validate(data=df.lazy()).col_vals_gt("x", 0, segments="region").interrogate()

Traceback

File ".../pointblank/validate.py", line 13391, in interrogate
    self._evaluate_segments(validation_info=self.validation_info)
File ".../pointblank/validate.py", line 18415, in _evaluate_segments
    for seg in seg_tuples:
               ^^^^^^^^^^
UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'seg_tuples' where it is not associated with a value

```

## Expected result

Segmented validation should behave the same on a  LazyFrame  as on a  DataFrame  (lazy inputs are supported per #192), collecting/materializing as needed to enumerate segment values.


## Development environment

* Linux
* pointblank 0.25.0 (latest release)
* polars 1.42.1
* Python 3.11

## Workaround

Calling  .collect()  on the frame before constructing  Validate  avoids it (segmented validation then runs on the eager frame).

Possibly related: #266 (another  _evaluate_segments  crash, with  seg_group  +  brief ) and #405 (another 0.25.0 lazy-path regression).

title: float_field: add a `precision` option to round generated values
description:
Currently `pb.float_field` generates full-precision floats (`rng.uniform(min_val, max_val)`), with no built-in way to control the number of decimals. The only workaround is a custom `generator=`, e.g. `pb.float_field(generator=lambda: round(rng.uniform(0, 100), 2))` — but that **replaces** the built-in generation, so it drops the ergonomics of `min_val`/`max_val`/`unique`/`nullable`/`null_probability`.

A first-class `precision: int | None = None` on `float_field` (rounding the value produced by `_generate_float` to N decimals) would compose cleanly with the existing constraints:

```python
pb.float_field(min_val=1.0, max_val=200.0, precision=2, unique=True)
# -> 27.74, 169.64, ...
```

Common use case: prices/scores. Happy to open a PR if the API shape sounds good.

title: Performance regression in 0.25.0: per-row checks on Polars LazyFrames are ~10× slower
description:
## Description

`col_vals_not_null` and `col_vals_le` on a Polars LazyFrame slowed down ~7-11× between
0.24.0 and 0.25.0. The regression is largest when the column has no failures (the
typical pass case), and scales linearly with row count.

Disclaimer: I used AI to format this issue and its associated MRE.

## Reproducible example

```python
import time
import polars as pl
import pointblank as pb

N = 2_000_000
lf = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "pk": pl.int_range(0, N, eager=True),
        "val": pl.int_range(0, N, eager=True),
    }
).lazy()


def t(label, fn):
    fn()  # warm-up
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    fn()
    print(f"  {label:20s} {time.perf_counter() - t0:.3f}s")


print(f"pointblank={pb.__version__}  polars={pl.__version__}  rows={N:,}")
t("col_vals_not_null", lambda: pb.Validate(data=lf).col_vals_not_null(columns="pk").interrogate())
t("col_vals_le",       lambda: pb.Validate(data=lf).col_vals_le(columns="val", value=N).interrogate())
t("rows_distinct",     lambda: pb.Validate(data=lf).rows_distinct(columns_subset=["pk"]).interrogate())
```

Run with:

```bash
uv run --with 'pointblank==0.24.0' --with 'polars==1.41.2' mre.py
uv run --with 'pointblank==0.25.0' --with 'polars==1.41.2' mre.py
```

## Result

Median of 3 iters on a 2M-row, ~46-column LazyFrame:

| check                          | 0.24.0  | 0.25.0  | slowdown |
|--------------------------------|--------:|--------:|---------:|
| `col_vals_not_null` ×3         | 0.007 s | 0.077 s | **11×**  |
| `col_vals_le` (date ≤ today)   | 0.004 s | 0.031 s | **8×**   |
| `rows_distinct` (composite PK) | 0.104 s | 0.142 s | 1.4×     |
| `col_schema_match`             | 0.017 s | 0.016 s | 1.0×     |


## Development environment

Tested on `polars==1.41.2`, Python 3.12, macOS arm64.

## Additional context

Add any other context about the problem here.

title: `rows_distinct()` silently excludes rows containing null values
description:
## Prework

- [x] Read and agree to the [code of conduct](https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct/) and [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).
- [x] If there is [already a relevant issue](https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/issues), whether open or closed, comment on the existing thread instead of posting a new issue.

## Description

`rows_distinct()` does not correctly assess distinctness for rows that contain null values in any of the checked columns. Rows with nulls are excluded from both PASS and FAIL counts, leading to misleading validation results.

In case of larger datasets, with many columns, most rows will have at least one null, making `rows_distinct()` on ALL COLUMNS nearly useless.

## Reproducible example

```python
import polars as pl
import pointblank as pb

df = pl.DataFrame({
    "id": ["A", "B", "C"],
    "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"],
    "score": [100, None, 100],
})

validation = (
    pb.Validate(data=df)
    .rows_distinct()                          # all columns
    .rows_distinct(columns_subset=["id"])     # only id column
    .interrogate()
)
validation
```

## Expected result

All 3 rows are distinct (different `id` values guarantee uniqueness). Both steps should report:
- UNITS: 3, PASS: 3, FAIL: 0

## Actual result

- **Step 1** (ALL COLUMNS): UNITS: 3, PASS: 2, FAIL: 0 — row B is excluded because `score` is null
- **Step 2** (`id` only): UNITS: 3, PASS: 3, FAIL: 0 — correct

## Environment

- pointblank: 0.24.0
- polars: 1.41.1
- narwhals: 2.21.2
- Python: 3.12 (Windows)

## Additional context

Add any other context about the problem here.

description:
## Prework

- [x] Read and abide by the Pointblank [code of conduct](https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct/) and [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).
- [x] Search for duplicates among the [existing issues](https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/issues) (both open and closed).

## Proposal

Continuing on the theme of multimodal inputs, I thought it'd be really cool if the `DraftValidation` class could support multimodal inputs (images and PDF), just as `Validate.prompt()` now does. A rough sketch of how that would work, drawing inspiration from the [How DraftValidation Works](https://posit-dev.github.io/pointblank/user-guide/advanced-validation/draft-validation.html#how-draftvalidation-works) steps:

1. A statistical summary of your data is generated using the [DataScan](https://posit-dev.github.io/pointblank/reference/DataScan.html#pointblank.DataScan) class.
2. This summary is converted to JSON format and sent to your selected LLM provider.
3. _NEW: You provide the `DraftValidation` class with an image or PDF file describing what the data should look like. For example, the image could be a schema diagram, while the PDF could outline the project configuration elements that the data should conform to._
4. The LLM uses the summary and multimodal input along with knowledge about Pointblank’s validation capabilities to generate a validation plan.
5. The result is returned as executable Python code that you can use directly or modify as needed

Happy to get feedback from you @rich-iannone, and iterate. I'd love to implement this.

title: Is collect() always necessary?
description:
## Question
**TLDR; does pointblank always intend to _collect_ dataframes in validation?** 

My team is wondering if there's a way to change pointblank's behavior so that it doesn't always collect the data frame when running validations. We think this might be a major lift, but maybe it's not as bad as we think. Some of our data sources are just too big to run `collect()`, but beyond that it creates some scalability concerns for us in our pipeline. Just wondering if there's room to modify that behavior over the mid to long-term, happy to discuss some of our ideas regarding how if that helps :)

As always, thanks for your work on this project, we're really enjoying using pointblank! 

### Background
Our team has been developing a kedro extension to use pointblank in our data pipeline, it works very nicely with the yaml workflow! We've been scaling pointblank across all of our datasets and we're starting to run into some problems due to `collect()`. 

Most of our data is pretty small, but some of it is _big_ (e.g. transaction data). Our pipeline uses a layered approach, earlier layers in the pipeline apply very general transformations to our data such as converting data types, modeling into 3rd normal form, etc. These layers don't use filters and we simply defer writes if the data is _large_. We simply return a deferred expression and subsequent layers in the pipeline can add new expressions to the chain. 

For the _big_ data, as a starting point we'd love to be able to run _table level assertions_ without relying on collect - things like schema enforcement at least help us insulate our later layers. Generally though, we're wondering if the validations could be passed to ibis as expressions and give us as end users more control over when / where data is collected.

title: Pointblank Python 3.14 Compatibility Issue
description:
# Pointblank Python 3.14 Compatibility Issue

**Issue Title:** `AttributeError: 'typing.Union' object attribute '__doc__' is read-only` in Python 3.14

**Repository:** https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank

**Environment:**
- Python Version: 3.14.0
- Pointblank Version: 0.15.0
- Operating System: Windows 10

**Description:**

The pointblank library fails to import in Python 3.14 with the following error:

```
AttributeError: 'typing.Union' object attribute '__doc__' is read-only
```

**Error Traceback:**
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test.py", line 1, in <module>
    import pointblank as pb
  File "...\pointblank\__init__.py", line 30, in <module>
    from pointblank.validate import (
  File "...\pointblank\validate.py", line 76, in <module>
    from pointblank._typing import SegmentSpec
  File "...\pointblank\_typing.py", line 31, in <module>
    Tolerance.__doc__ = "Tolerance (i.e., the allowed deviation)"
    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AttributeError: 'typing.Union' object attribute '__doc__' is read-only
```

**Root Cause:**

In Python 3.14, the `__doc__` attribute on `typing.Union` objects became read-only. The pointblank library attempts to set `Tolerance.__doc__` on line 31 of `_typing.py`, which fails.

**Affected Code Location:**
- File: `pointblank/_typing.py`
- Line: 31
- Code: `Tolerance.__doc__ = "Tolerance (i.e., the allowed deviation)"`

**Expected Behavior:**
The library should import successfully in Python 3.14.

**Suggested Fix:**

Wrap the `__doc__` assignment in a try-except block to handle the AttributeError gracefully:

```python
# Before (fails in Python 3.14):
Tolerance.__doc__ = "Tolerance (i.e., the allowed deviation)"

# After (compatible with Python 3.14+):
try:
    Tolerance.__doc__ = "Tolerance (i.e., the allowed deviation)"
except AttributeError:
    # __doc__ is read-only on typing.Union in Python 3.14+, skip assignment
    pass
```

**Workaround:**

A workaround script has been created that patches the library automatically. The patch:
1. Finds the pointblank installation
2. Backs up the original `_typing.py` file
3. Wraps the `__doc__` assignment in a try-except block

**Testing:**
- Tested with Python 3.14.0
- pointblank version 0.15.0
- Works with the patch applied

**Additional Notes:**
- This is a breaking change in Python 3.14's typing module
- The workaround is backward compatible with Python 3.11 and 3.12
- The patch can be applied automatically via a script

title: feat: Execute on Ibis backend via Narwhals
description:
## Prework

- [x] Read and abide by the Pointblank [code of conduct](https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct/) and [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/blob/main/.github/CONTRIBUTING.md).
- [x] Search for duplicates among the [existing issues](https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/issues) (both open and closed).

## Proposal
### Currently
Currently, Pointblank handles Ibis tables and columns by converting them to polars or pandas. This means:

1. Data is on backend (DuckDB, Snowflake, etc.)
2. Data is loaded into memory via Ibis to Polars
3. Checks are evaluated eagerly in-memory via Polars 
4. Checks report is available in-memory

### Proposed feature
#192 requests LazyFrame support for Polars lazy execution. Once that's supported, it should be trivial to add lazy support for Narwhals. Via the recent [Narwhals-Ibis integration](https://github.com/narwhals-dev/narwhals/pull/2000), it should be possible to execute checks on-backend. Meaning we would have:

1. Construct a query plan from all lazy checks via Narwhals (polars-compatible API)
2. Pass the Ibis Table reference to the query plan
3. The query plan is executed on-backend via Ibis; the full dataset never leaves memory
4. The query plan results are loaded into memory (i.e., checks report) 

This Narwhals-Ibis bridge enables on-backend compute for most features (e.g., DataScan)

title: feat: extend segmentation to allow grouping of values in a column
description:
Right now, we can either create segments from:

- all distinct values in a column
- specific values in a column

Here's an example for the latter case:

```python
(
    pb.Validate(
        data=pb.load_dataset(),
        tbl_name="small_table",
        label="Segmented validation on specific categories"
    )
    .col_vals_gt(
        columns="d",
        value=100,
        segments=("f", ["low", "high"])  # Only segment on "low" and "high" values in column `f`
    )
    .interrogate()
)
```

It would be nice to extend this so that we might create a segment based on *both* the `"low"` and `"high"` values. Perhaps this could be done with a helper function, like this:

```python
(
    pb.Validate(
        data=pb.load_dataset(),
        tbl_name="small_table",
        label="Segmented validation on specific categories"
    )
    .col_vals_gt(
        columns="d",
        value=100,
        segments=("f", pb.seg_group("low", "high"))  # Group "low" and "high" from `f` into a single segment
    )
    .interrogate()
)
```

Using helper functions like this might be good because in the future we might extend further with more `seg_*()` functions like:

- `seg_range()`: create named segments from ranges of values
- `seg_fn()`:  apply a custom function to create segments
- `seg_quantile()`: create segments based on quantiles

title: feat: have comparison validations work with fixed dates/datetimes
description:
With https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/pull/110, basic support for column-column comparison validations with dates and datetimes was made possible. The next piece to support is date/datetime comparison using a fixed date/datetime value. Here is the motivating example:

```python
import pointblank as pb
import polars as pl
import datetime


pl_df = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "date_1": ["2021-01-01", "2021-02-01"],
        "date_2": ["2021-02-01", "2021-03-01"],
        "dttm_1": ["2021-01-01 02:30:00", "2021-02-01 02:30:00"],
        "dttm_2": ["2021-02-01 03:30:00", "2021-03-01 03:30:00"],
    }
)

pl_df = pl_df.with_columns(
    [
        pl.col("date_1").str.to_date(),
        pl.col("date_2").str.to_date(),
        pl.col("dttm_1").str.to_datetime(),
        pl.col("dttm_2").str.to_datetime(),
    ]
)

validation = (
    pb.Validate(data=pl_df)
    .col_vals_ge(columns="date_1", value=datetime.date(2021, 1, 1))
    .interrogate()
)

validation
```

For this we'd want the value to be a `datetime` date or datetime and not require the use of DataFrame specific expression of a date or datetime.

title: Pass string template inputs to Actions Callable for more flexible/generic actions
description:
## Prework

- [X] Read and abide by the pointblank [code of conduct](https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct/) and [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/blob/main/.github/CONTRIBUTING.md).
- [X] Search for duplicates among the [existing issues](https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/issues) (both open and closed).

## Proposal

I am trying to integrate pointblank validation with enterprise alerting tools by writing a custom `Callable` and passing it to Actions. However, in Callable mode, there does not seem to be access to the string templating parameters, i.e. https://posit-dev.github.io/pointblank/reference/Actions.html#string-templating
Without those, it's difficult to implement meaningful custom alerting - a separate function needs to be configured for each check, rather that one implementation that can work for all of them. 

I propose that a dict or dataclass of these parameters is passed to the Callable, i.e. something like this
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
import pointblank as pb

@dataclass
class ActionParams:
    type: str
    level: Literal["warning", "error", "critical"]
    step: int
    column: str
    val: Any
    time: datetime

def log_issue(params: ActionParams):
    log_level=getattr(logging, params.level.upper())
    log.log(log_level, "'%s' threshold exceeded for column %s.", params.type, params.column)

validation = (
    pb.Validate(
        data=pb.load_dataset(dataset="game_revenue", tbl_type="duckdb"),
        thresholds=pb.Thresholds(warning=0.05, error=0.10, critical=0.15),
        # Only register actions once
        actions=pb.Actions(warning=log_issue, error=log_issue, critical=log_issue)
    )
    .col_vals_regex(columns="player_id", pattern=r"[A-Z]{12}\d{3}")
    .col_vals_gt(columns="item_revenue", value=0.05)
    .col_vals_gt(
        columns="session_duration",
        value=15,
    )
    .interrogate()
)

validation
```

In addition to facilitating logging, other alerting API's could then be more easily plugged in.

title: feat: add ability to use a subset of columns for step reports

We'll always include the row numbers on the left-hand side. And the target column should always be present (otherwise, what's the point?). An interesting thing to try is to have a way (special string like `":target:"`?) that can be used to order the target column with the other chosen columns.

title: Customization of title and columns included in `get_step_report`
description:
## Prework

- [X] Read and abide by the pointblank [code of conduct](https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct/) and [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/blob/main/.github/CONTRIBUTING.md).
- [X] Search for duplicates among the [existing issues](https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/issues) (both open and closed).

## Proposal

I understand that `get_step_report` is still experimental, but have found them to be super useful so far. Two ideas for improving the step reports:
 - Be able to customize the title of the step report, similar to the `title` argument for `get_tabular_report`. The titles are currently hard-coded in a number of places. I tried to replace the title on the GT result directly, but it looks like GT doesn't have a public API for this (but can hack around it).
 - Optionally be able to customize the columns included in the row-based step report. For wide tables (i.e. 100+ columns) it would be great to specify a handful of key identifying columns, and then add in the test columns to the table. The default behavior could remain unchanged. I considered trying to do this on the resulting GT table directly, but there are two problems. 
   - The first is that while GT does have an API to hide columns, it doesn't have a public API to list all the column, so it's tricky to figure out the columns I want to hide - I'd rather specify which ones to include. 
   - The second is that the table objects in the output objects end up being much larger than they really need to be.
  
Below is a snippet of code I used to hack around both of these for now.
```
        try:
            report = validation.get_step_report(i)
        except ValueError:  # Step report for col_exists(columns="foo") will raise if "foo" doesn't exist
            report = None
        validation_info = validation.validation_info[i - 1]
        if report is not None:  # Some types of checks don't have reports
            if self.columns is not None and validation_info.assertion_type in ROW_BASED_VALIDATION_TYPES:
                # No public API to get the full list of columns, so we have to get use the private API
                all_columns = [col.var for col in report._boxhead]
                # Make sure to always keep the validation column
                columns_to_keep = self.columns + [validation_info.column]
                columns_to_hide = [col for col in all_columns if col not in columns_to_keep]
                if columns_to_hide:
                    report = report.cols_hide(columns=columns_to_hide)
            if self.title is not None:
                # Add the title to the report via a bit of GT hackery. This is not a public API but it works for now.
                from great_tables import html

                title = html(self.title.format(step=i))
                report = report.tab_header(title=title, subtitle=report._heading.subtitle, preheader=report._heading.preheader)
            return report
```

## Proposal

Add the ability to use comparison validation functions (`col_vals_ge`, `col_vals_le`, etc.) to work on date types.

---

## Examples

| Project        | Start Date  | End Date    |
|--------------|------------|------------|
| Project Alpha | 2024-01-01 | 2024-04-01 |
| Project Beta  | 2024-02-01 | 2024-05-01 |
| Project Gamma | 2024-03-01 | 2024-06-01 |
| Project Delta | 2024-04-01 | 2024-07-01 |

### Current State

I have to write a function to convert the dates to epoch time so I can compare them as numbers.

```python
import pointblank as pb
import pandas as pd

sample = pd.DataFrame({
    "Project": ["Project Alpha", "Project Beta", "Project Gamma", "Project Delta"],
    "Start Date": pd.to_datetime(["2024-01-01", "2024-02-01", "2024-03-01", "2024-04-01"]),
    "End Date": pd.to_datetime(["2024-04-01", "2024-05-01", "2024-06-01", "2024-07-01"])
})

validation = (
    pb.Validate(data=sample)
    .col_vals_ge(
        columns='Start Date',
        value=pb.col('End Date'),
        pre=lambda df: df.apply(lambda col: col.astype('int64') if pd.api.types.is_datetime64_any_dtype(col) else col)
    )
    .interrogate()
)

validation
```

Date types are supported without any additional conversion needed.


```python

sample = pd.DataFrame({

## Prework

- [X] Search for duplicates among the [existing issues](https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/issues) (both open and closed).

## Proposal

Great library! Thank you for all the work on it so far.

When including multiple custom column expressions (`col_vals_expr`) as steps, it becomes very difficult to tell them apart in `get_tabular_report`. 

* It would be helpful if the "columns" field was populated, i.e. via `pl.Expr.meta.root_names()`. This looks similar to what is available in the R version (rstudio/pointblank#570)
* It would be helpful if the "step" column included the output name of the expression, if provided. i.e.
`(pl.col("a") % 1==0).alias("a_mod_1")` would display as `col_vals_expr(a_mod_1)` instead of just `col_vals_expr()`. For polars, this can be done via `pl.Expr.meta.output_name()`.
* In addition, since every step has a "brief" input, it would be nice to have an option in `Validate.get_tabular_report` to add a column that displays these inputs across all steps. This would also help to relabel steps that use `col_vals_regex` once the regular expressions become too complicated to be intuitive to consumers of the report.

This part will be difficult, there are 3 ways I think it can happen. First, is using some sort of exception logic like `from a except b` - blunt and useful. Second, using some row hashing functionality and then excepting the second from the first. Third would be using a join key(s), which I feel data will commonly have, and using one of the first 2 strategies from there, probably the hashing.

I've experimented on my own side in a professional setting with all of the 3. I find the exception method very easy but I strictly use duckdb for that. When I'm getting fancy or have some non-trivial join key logic I use the hashing but much to my dismay as it's usually categorically worse.

What I've had horrible experiences with is sorting join keys. I'm looking for a solution that can sort out of memory on quite large datasets, and I can't find a good solution that pre-sorts.

There are downsides to all these approaches and I think Narwhals will need some contributions in order to get this to work in a general sense. Polars has has hashing logic and duckdb has exception logic, can't speak for everything else.

## Proposal

It would be very useful to have the `is_exact()` argument in the `col_schema_match()` method, so that one can run validations only on the dataframe columns regardless of the type.

An alternative would be to allow for multiple dtypes of a column, so for example:

```python
schema = pb.Schema(
    columns=[("a", ("String"|"Null")), ("b", "Int64"), ("c", "Float64")]
)
```

title: `Validate.col_schema_match()` seems to use narwhals typing when original DF is pandas
description:
This is a problem because the types aren't the same after the conversion to a narwhals DF

```python
import pandas as pd
import narwhals as nw

df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': [3, 4]})
print(df.dtypes)
#> A    int64
#> B    int64
#> dtype: object

dfnw = nw.from_native(df)
print(dfnw.schema)

#> Schema({'A': Int64, 'B': Int64})
```

https://github.com/rich-iannone/pointblank/blob/0e3d7417b954019aee9f1b7e2c61d6bc571468f7/tests/test_schema.py#L91-L119

title: Collect detailed information from interrogation on `col_schema_match()`
description:
The `col_schema_match()` validation method has a large number of options for flexibly performing schema checks. With a single test unit, we can determine whether the schema check passed or failed.

While it’s good that this functionality works, there is a problem. When a schema check fails, the user gets no information on how the check failed for the parameters chosen. This is not ideal because then the onus is on the user to figure out what exactly caused the failure. Thus, we ought to collected detailed information on what passed and what failed with regard to schema checking at interrogation time.

title: Move dev dependencies to `[dependency-groups]`
description:
[PEP 735](https://peps.python.org/pep-0735/) was accepted and now there's a place for all the dependencies that are not meant to be installed as core or optional dependencies (e.g. `[uv] pip install 'pointblank[sql]'`). You would just need to replace `[project.optional-dependencies]` with `[dependency-groups]` here.

[ref](https://github.com/rich-iannone/pointblank/blob/4618f0d76a5bd0ba15fa07b04e7076c369ade7d4/pyproject.toml#L47C1-L64C2)

In case you use uv, it [already supports this](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/dependencies/#dependency-groups), so if you do `uv add --dev` this is the default place where these will end up.

This also enables you to split dev dependencies from docs, benchmarks, etc.

By the way, sick project!

title: bug(dependencies): Unused `mcp[cli]` dependency resolves to mcp 2.0.0 and breaks "import fastmcp"
description:
## Summary `pointblank` declares a direct dependency on the `mcp` SDK (`mcp[cli]>=1.10.1`) in both the `mcp` extra and the `dev` dependency group, but no code in the repository imports `mcp` directly. Since `mcp` 2.0.0 was published (on 2026-07-28), that unused and unbounded requirement causes any fresh dependency resolution to produce an environment where `import fastmcp` fails. 1. `mcp` 2.0.0 is a [breaking rewrite](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/releases). It renames `McpError` to `MCPError` and drops `pydantic-settings` from its runtime dependencies. 2. `fastmcp` 2.14.0 and 2.14.1 declare `mcp` with no upper bound (`mcp>=1.23.1` and `mcp>=1.24.0`), and `fastmcp/settings.py` imports `pydantic_settings` without declaring it, relying on `mcp<2` to supply it transitively. FastMCP restored the `mcp<2.0` cap in 2.14.2. 3. `pointblank` requires `mcp[cli]>=1.10.1` directly and unbounded. The resolver maximizes that direct requirement to `mcp==2.0.0`, then backtracks `fastmcp` to 2.14.1, the newest release whose `mcp` range still admits 2.0.0. That pairing is broken.
FastMCP `mcp` bounds

| fastmcp | declared `mcp` bound | safe | |---|---|---| | 2.11.3 to 2.13.x | `mcp<2.0.0` | yes | | **2.14.0, 2.14.1** | **unbounded** | **no** | | 2.14.2 to 2.14.7 | `mcp<2.0` | yes | | 3.x (via `fastmcp-slim`) | `mcp<2.0`, and declares `pydantic-settings` directly | yes |

(Specific version search was performed with help of Claude Opus 5.0) ## Proposed fix Drop the unused `mcp` SDK requirement and let FastMCP own its own `mcp` bound. The `>=2.14.2` floor is the release that restored the `mcp<2.0` cap. ```diff -mcp = ["mcp[cli]>=1.10.1", "fastmcp>=2.11.3", "pytest-asyncio>=1.0.0"] +mcp = ["fastmcp>=2.14.2", "pytest-asyncio>=1.0.0"] [dependency-groups] dev = [ - "mcp[cli]>=1.10.1", - "fastmcp>=2.10.5", + "fastmcp>=2.14.2", ] ``` --- Spotted in Narwhals downstream test (see [failing job](https://github.com/narwhals-dev/narwhals/actions/runs/30701344185/job/91372774418?pr=3827))
